content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler food, NFS (262) is a ready‑to‑eat baby product designed for children aged 6 months to 3 years. It is made from carefully selected ingredients, contains no artificial additives, and is suitable for daily consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Developed in accordance with pediatric and nutritionist recommendations.
Provides a balanced ratio of protein, fat, and carbohydrates needed for growth and development.
Contains only natural, non‑GMO ingredients.
Packaged in safe material that preserves freshness.
Undergoes strict quality control and meets international baby‑food standards.

items.title: Supports growth
items.content: Rich in essential vitamins and minerals such as vitamin D, calcium, and iron, which support healthy bone development and overall growth.

items.title: Brain development
items.content: Enriched with DHA and other omega‑3 fatty acids important for nervous system and cognitive function development.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C and zinc help maintain immune protection during rapid growth phases.

items.title: Easy digestion
items.content: Formulated for quick absorption by the infant’s gastrointestinal tract.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Contains prebiotics that promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: If the child is allergic to any ingredient, use the product with caution.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: After opening, store the product in the refrigerator and consume within the indicated period.

items.title: Not for children over 3 years
items.content: The product is intended for children up to 3 years; older children should use age‑appropriate nutrition.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve at room temperature. Before serving, you may gently warm it in warm water. For infants under 1 year, offer small portions and gradually increase the amount.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place. After opening, keep refrigerated at 2 °C–8 °C and use within 48 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain cheese crackers are crunchy biscuits made from whole grain flour (such as wheat, rye or oat) topped with a thin layer of grated cheese. They have a rich cheesy flavor, a hint of salt and the nutty aroma of whole grains.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain crackers retain bran and germ, making them more nutritious than refined white crackers.
The cheese topping is often made from Parmesan or cheddar, adding extra calcium.
Traditionally these crackers were a lightweight source of energy and protein for hikers.
In some countries they are served with soups and salads as a crunchy garnish.
Manufacturers sometimes add seeds (sunflower, pumpkin) for extra flavor and texture.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grains keep the bran, which supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The cheese layer contributes calcium important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Contains plant protein
items.content: Both the grain base and cheese provide modest amounts of protein for tissue repair.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: Unlike sweet snacks, these crackers contain virtually no sugar, making them suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: Provides B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole grains supply thiamine, niacin and folate, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The cheese topping can trigger reactions in people allergic to dairy proteins.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese and added salt may increase sodium levels, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: If wheat or rye flour is used, the product contains gluten and is not suitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese crackers are convenient as a snack on their own, served alongside soups or salads, or used as a base for canapés with spreads and vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store in the refrigerator to maintain crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: The Double Hamburger is a classic fast‑food item consisting of two large beef patties (171 g each), a bun, cheese, lettuce, tomato, onion, pickles and sauce. It is designed for those who want a richer taste and a bigger protein portion in a single meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Double hamburgers are often featured in limited‑time promotions to draw attention to new menu items.
Each 171‑g patty provides roughly 340 g of pure meat in total, nearly double the weight of a standard single hamburger.
In some countries the double burger is served with a double layer of cheese, pushing the calorie count to 900 kcal or more.
The bun for a double burger is usually sturdier to hold the extra weight of the patties.
During the 2020s many fast‑food chains began testing plant‑based double burgers as a vegetarian alternative.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Two beef patties deliver about 50 g of protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef provides heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The patties contain vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, which aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: The cheese slice adds calcium essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Dietary fiber from vegetables
items.content: Lettuce, tomato and onion contribute a modest amount of fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: High calorie count
items.content: A double hamburger can contain 800–1100 kcal, making it unsuitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Saturated fat load
items.content: Beef patties and cheese are rich in saturated fats, which can raise cholesterol when consumed excessively.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Sauces and pickles add significant sodium, a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Gluten in the bun, dairy in the cheese, and possible additives may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: When purchasing from non‑certified outlets, verify the beef source to avoid food‑borne illness risks.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The double hamburger is typically served in a paper wrapper and eaten by hand. You can add extra sauce or spices to taste. For a healthier twist, swap the bun for a whole‑grain version and load up on additional fresh vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared double hamburger in the refrigerator for no more than 2–3 days at 4 °C. For longer keeping, freeze it, where it retains quality for up to 1 month. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Mackerel (Scomber scombrus) is a marine fish from the Scombridae family, found in temperate and subtropical waters of the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Fried mackerel is usually prepared whole after gutting, lightly coated in flour or breadcrumbs, and pan‑fried until golden. It has a rich aroma, firm flesh with a pronounced, oily flavor, and is high in omega‑3 fatty acids.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mackerel can migrate over 3,000 km in search of food and spawning grounds.
Unlike many other fish, mackerel grows quickly, reaching up to 1.5 kg in a single season.
Its oily flesh makes it popular worldwide, from Japanese sashimi to Mediterranean fried fillets.
Mackerel is considered an indicator species for water quality because its populations are sensitive to pollution.
In Russia, fried mackerel is a staple in traditional fish restaurants.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Omega‑3s support heart health, lower triglyceride levels, and have anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Provides all essential amino acids, making it an excellent source for muscle repair and maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: selenium and iodine
items.content: Selenium protects cells from oxidative stress, while iodine is essential for thyroid health.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Vitamin A and DHA in mackerel contribute to good vision.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Like many larger marine fish, mackerel can contain trace amounts of mercury; pregnant women and young children should limit intake.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including mackerel.

items.title: High sodium when seasoned
items.content: Using salt or sauces can raise sodium levels, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Frying oil considerations
items.content: Choose an oil with a high smoke point to avoid formation of harmful trans fats during frying.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fried mackerel hot, often with lemon wedges, fresh herbs, or tartar sauce. It can be eaten as a main dish, added to salads, pastas, or used in sandwiches. For a lighter option, skip the breadcrumb coating and simply pan‑fry the fillet in olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked fried mackerel in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 2 months. Reheat in the oven or skillet before serving to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Pie, oatmeal is a baked dessert made from a crust and a filling of oatmeal, milk, eggs and sugar. Often fruit, nuts or spices are added. The result is a tender crumb with a fragrant, mildly sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oat flakes in the filling make the pie more nutritious and give it a characteristic nutty aroma.
Traditionally this pie is prepared in the autumn, when oats are harvested in large quantities.
In some regions honey is used instead of sugar in the dough, adding a distinct taste note.
Oatmeal pie is commonly served with tea or coffee as a light dessert.
Oats are considered a symbol of abundance and well‑being in several cultures.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Oat flakes provide soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of slow‑release carbs
items.content: The starch in oats is released gradually, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains beta‑glucans
items.content: Beta‑glucans can lower cholesterol and support the immune system.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Oats supply B1, B5 and folate, essential for metabolic processes.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The pie provides magnesium, iron and zinc, which aid muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: If wheat flour is used in the crust, the product may be unsafe for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweet versions can contribute to weight gain when consumed in excess.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: The crust and butter make the pie calorie‑dense, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Added additives
items.content: Some recipes include artificial flavors or preservatives that may trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the oatmeal pie warm or at room temperature. It can be enjoyed on its own or paired with yogurt, fresh berries or ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the pie in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage refrigerate up to 5 days, or freeze and reheat in the oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Roll, garlic is a soft bun made from wheat flour, yeast, water and a pinch of salt, filled with fragrant garlic butter. It is popular in Asian and European cuisines as a quick snack or side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Garlic rolls are often served in sushi restaurants as bite‑size portions.
The classic recipe mixes butter, minced garlic and sometimes herbs such as parsley or dill.
In Japan a similar product is called “naru” and is frequently used in bento boxes.
Garlic intensifies aroma while keeping the dough’s tender texture.
Garlic rolls can be sweet (with honey) or spicy (with chili).

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Garlic contains allicin and other compounds that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports immune system
items.content: Regular consumption of garlic may boost the body’s defenses.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough provides B1, B3 and folate, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: The roll offers quickly digestible energy, useful before physical activity.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When made with a moderate amount of butter, the roll remains relatively low‑fat.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity may react to the roll.

items.title: Strong garlic odor
items.content: The potent smell can be unpleasant in confined spaces.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salt is added to the dough, watch daily sodium intake.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: Garlic may cause heartburn or stomach upset in some individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Garlic roll can be enjoyed warm, split in half and brushed with extra garlic butter. It is often served with soy sauce, mayo or fresh vegetables. Perfect as a snack or accompaniment to soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep rolls in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze for up to 2 months. Warm before eating in an oven or microwave.
